name: soninké
confidence_why: Creissels 2016, a full phonology of Kingi Soninke with lexical tonal minimal pairs, together with Diagne 2006 on Bakel Soninke and Y. Diagana 1990, describes a two-tone system with no word stress; the only dissent is Platiel 1981, an early and self-described tentative analysis, written before the tonal nature of Soninke was established, which took the tones for relics and posited a syllable-structure-driven intensity accent instead.

catalog_quote: En faisant abstraction de la modulation descendante dont il sera question en 3.3, chaque syllabe d’un mot en soninké du Kingi est caractérisable comme ou bien haute (H) ou bien basse (B). On discutera plus loin la possibilité d’analyser ce système comme un système à ton bas marqué ... Une caractéristique remarquable de ce système tonal est que rien dans la distribution des tons ou dans les processus tonals ne demande de reconnaître des propriétés tonales différentes aux différents types de syllabes. sweep_summary: Two title hits, neither readable online. (1) Borges 2009, Leiden MA thesis 'Some prosodic features of Soninke of Gambia', 121 pp.: print only (Leiden UB Closed Stack 3, 8553 A 42; OCLC 778344413; not in the Leiden student-theses repository, no Google Books preview). Relevance unclear from the title, but it is the only first-hand prosodic study of a western (Gambian) variety, and Creissels (2015 p.2, 2016 pp.5/27-28) says western varieties may have substantially different prosodic systems and Bakel may be losing tone — so high acquisition priority as a possible variety-level refinement. (2) Rialland 1991, Linguistique Africaine 7: 117-124, her reply to Creissels 1991 'Remarques sur le système tonal du soninké' defending Rialland 1990 'Le système prosodique du soninké' (HAL metadata only, keyword Tonology): a tonological debate on Kaédi Soninke, not a stress description; print only, low priority. Nothing found contradicts the 'tonal' coding. New first-hand text read: Creissels 2015 CALL paper (author's site) states 'Kingi Soninke has two contrastive level tones, H and L' with no stress/accent — confirms, does not supersede Creissels 2016. findings rest on Glottolog, HAL, Crossref, Leiden Primo, LPP, Google Books and Creissels' site downloads.

new_statements.translation: [p. 99:] In words of structure CVCV or CVNCV only tendencies are found; the differences, where there are any, bear on the place of the intensity accent rather than on the tonal pitch register. [p. 100:] In words of structure CVVCV or CVCCV the tone/accent marks are, on the contrary, perfectly clear and remain constant: a) CVVCV is always accented on the 1st syllable, low register; b) CVCCV is always accented on the 1st syllable, high register [...] it appears certain that Soninke must have been a tone language opposing two registers [...] its tonal distinctions are combined with an intensity accent.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog and Creissels 2015 code Soninke as a tone language with contrastive H vs. L on every syllable (lexical minimal pairs) and mention no stress. Platiel instead holds that the tonal system has lost its distinctive character (only traces survive) and that the language has an intensity accent whose placement is conditioned by syllable structure (heavy CVV or pre-geminate syllable), with lexically variable placement in CVCV words. Both the type (accent vs. contrastive tone) and the existence of word stress differ. Her data come from her own materials and the DNAFLA Soninke-French lexicon (Mali, 1979; note 2 p. 106), i.e. Malian Soninke; note 3 (p. 106) records that Diagana's 1980 Paris…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Platiel treats Soninke as a former two-register tone language whose tonal oppositions have lost most of their distinctive value, combined with an intensity accent (stress); a word carries a single accent except in compounds (p. 95). Its place is fixed by syllable structure: a word with a long vowel (CVVCV) is always stressed on that first, heavy syllable, with low register; a word with a geminate (CVCCV) is always stressed on the syllable before the geminate, i.e. the first, with high register (p. 80: 'CCV : accent d'intensité de registre haut frappant, non pas cette syllabe mais celle qui la précède'); CVCV words show only tendencies, splitting into three lexical groups (stress on the 1st syllable, on the 2nd, or no stress, all high register) with only exceptional minimal pairs; CVNCV words never stress the first syllable and show at most a weak high-register stress on the second in slow careful speech. Tri- and quadrisyllables follow the same rules according to where CVV or CC sits (p. 99).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'à l'exception des mots composés, un mot ne peut porter qu'un seul accent d'intensité' (p. 95); compounds may carry more than one.
new_statements.exceptions: CVCV words: three lexical groups differing in accent place (1st syllable, 2nd syllable, none), with rare minimal pairs and many doublets (p. 99); CVNCV words: no accent on the first syllable, only a very weak one on the second (pp. 99-100); nine monosyllabic grammatical words and about 30 Arabic loans with initial a-/al- fall outside the syllable canon (pp. 80-81). Platiel adds that the distinctive use of tonal and accentual oppositions 'n'est maintenant utilisé que très exceptionnellement' (p. 105).

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog and Creissels 2015: a two-level tone language with lexical tonal contrasts on noun bases; no word stress posited. Adds that an earlier first-hand description (O. Diagana 1980, 1984, Kaédi, Mauritania; not opened) analysed the language as tone plus accent. Variety of the author's own data not named in the article.
new_statements.rule_in_words: An autosegmental analysis of noun-phrase tone: Soninke is a two-tone (H, B=L) language; noun bases carry one of four base tonal schemes (B, BH, HB, H), number morphemes are H, determiners B, BHB or H, and surface melodies follow from tone-to-nucleus association within tonal domains defined by the determiner. Nothing is said about stress or accent for the author's own analysis; the only mention of accent is in note 1, reporting that Ousmane Diagana (1980 thesis and 1984 thèse d'Etat on the Soninke of Kaédi, Mauritania) treated Soninke as 'une langue à ton et à accent', an analysis the author explicitly sets aside.

tone_statements.citation: Vydrin, Valentin. 2024 [version 2.1, deposited 17 Feb 2025]. Eastern Soninke. Analytical report on the tonal system (ERC project 'Theory of Tone' (ThoT) analytical reports, questionnaire version 8b). Zenodo. doi:10.5281/zenodo.14884871 (all versions: 10.5281/zenodo.14725392). 1 docx file, c. 45 pp. of text.
tone_statements.quote: Soninke has two level tones: high and low. The only contour tone is HL, it is available on the final syllable of a definite noun before a pause, if the preceding syllable carries a low tone, or in monosyllabic nouns: yàxàrê ‘woman’, sèrê ‘human, person’, sî ‘horse’. ... Two level tonemes can be postulated in Soninke, L and H. ... The HL contour should be interpreted as a combination of two level tonemes, H and L
tone_statements.locator: §3.1 'Character of tonal system', §3.2.1 'Tonemes L and H', §3.2.3 'The non-tonemic status of the HL contour' (docx, no page numbers in the text; c. pp. 4-5)
tone_statements.summary: Two level tonemes L and H ('omnitonal', contra Creissels' H = zero); HL fall only derived (floating L of definite article); only L floats; downstep H!H from floating L, downdrift; word patterns H, LH, HL, HLH.. mapped by span rules; no stress. Data: Creissels 2016 (Kingi); 200+ tone-marked forms.

tone_statements.citation: Green, Christopher R. & Maria Konoshenko. 2022. Tonal head marking in Mande compounds: endpoint neutralization and outliers. Mandenkan 67: 3-44. doi:10.4000/mandenkan.2699
tone_statements.quote: Unlike Bozo, a great deal is known about Soninke [iso:snk] and its tonal behavior. Contrary to most other languages discussed so far, in Kingi Soninke, W2 does not neutralize in compounds, as shown in (17). [...] Lack of W2 neutralization in these instances may suggest that Soninke is an outlier with respect to THM. However, THM does occur elsewhere in Soninke, such as in canonical possessive constructions with a referential possessor (18). In possessive constructions, a monosyllabic W2's tone polarizes against W1 as shown in (18a,b), while a non-monosyllabic W2 receives replacive {LH}, cf. (18c,d).
tone_statements.locator: section 4.3 (outliers), paragraphs 66-68 of the OpenEdition HTML (print pp. 3-44), exx. (17)-(18)

tone_statements.citation: Creissels, Denis. 2018. Le rôle du ton dans la morphologie flexionnelle du soninké (mandé ouest). In Jean Léo Léonard & Annie Rialland (éds.), Linguistique africaine: perspectives croisées (Journées scientifiques de la Société de Linguistique de Paris, 23 janvier 2016), 163-187. Paris: Éditions de la Société de Linguistique de Paris. ISBN 979-10-699-2586-1.
tone_statements.quote: Comme cela est illustré en (4), le soninké du Kingi a une opposition tonale binaire H vs. B. [...] Ce système présente deux caractéristiques typologiques majeures : (a) En soninké du Kingi, l'unité porteuse de ton est la syllabe, [...] on ne relève aucune différence de comportement entre des syllabes 'légères' et des syllabes 'lourdes'. (b) Le système tonal du soninké du Kingi [...] est un système à ton B marqué, dont on peut simplifier la description en posant que seuls les tons B sont spécifiés en structure sous-jacente, les tons H étant assignés par défaut aux syllabes qui n'ont pas été atteintes par l'expansion d'un domaine de ton bas.
tone_statements.translation: As illustrated in (4), Kingi Soninke has a binary tonal opposition H vs L. [...] This system has two major typological characteristics: (a) in Kingi Soninke the tone-bearing unit is the syllable, [...] there is no difference in behaviour between 'light' and 'heavy' syllables; (b) the Kingi Soninke tone system [...] is a marked-L system, whose description can be simplified by positing that only L tones are specified underlyingly, H tones being assigned by default to syllables not reached by the spreading of a low-tone domain.
tone_statements.locator: §3.1 'Ton haut et ton bas', pp. 167-168 (the H vs. B sentence and ex. (4) on p. 167; the (a)/(b) typological characteristics on p. 168)

tone_statements.citation: Green, Christopher R. 2018. A survey of word-level replacive tonal patterns in Western Mande. Mandenkan 59: 67-108. doi:10.4000/mandenkan.1420
tone_statements.quote: In each instance, unlike what we have come to expect in most Central and Southwestern Mande compounds, in Kingi Soninke, the lexical tonal melody of W2 in a compound is maintained in its entirety, while that of W1 is clearly neutralized. [...] These Kingi Soninke data show, however, that the tonal melody of W1 is always neutralized in favor of its initial tone. For example, in (32a), W1's /LLHL/ melody is neutralized to [LLL], while in (32d), W1's /HLHL/ is neutralized to [HHH]. [...] Thus, in every instance, the neutralized melody of W1 is either all‑H or all‑L, while the melody of W2 is maintained.
tone_statements.locator: section 'Soninke-Bozo', paragraph 128 of the OpenEdition HTML (print pp. 67-108), after ex. (32)

readall_conflicts: One real disagreement. Platiel 1981 (Malian data: her own materials plus the DNAFLA lexicon) holds that Soninke's two-register tone system has lost its distinctive character and that the language carries an intensity accent, one per word, placed by syllable structure (always on the long-vowel syllable of CVVCV, low register; always on the syllable before a geminate in CVCCV, high register; lexically variable and weak in CVCV, absent on the first syllable of CVNCV). Against this, Creissels 2015 (Kingi, Mali) and Y. Diagana 1990 analyse Soninke as a two-tone language with lexical tonal contrasts and never mention stress, and Halaouï 1990 (Mauritania) simply marks tones. Y. Diagana's note 1 records a third position, O. Diagana's (Kaédi, Mauritania, 1980/1984) 'langue à ton et à accent', not opened here. Rialland 1991, which by its title answers Creissels on exactly this prosodic question, could not be opened. Diagana 1985 and both Grégoire articles are silent.

sources.quote: Bakel Soninke data. Ch.6 analyses a tone system: roots carry a tonal plane, non-root morphemes are lexically toneless and get tone by spreading/floating-tone assignment/default H; three purely tonal morphemes (floating L 'complétude' suffix causing downstep or final falling contour; two L boundary prefixes). §6.2: 'Lexicalement le système soninké est à registre marqué bas' with lexical inventory H and L and a surface mid-high tone from downstep. No word stress/accent anywhere (the only 'accent' hit in the text is non-prosodic).

sources.citation: Platiel, Susanne (1981). Phonologie soninké : une tentative d'analyse dynamique. Mandenkan: bull. semestriel d'études linguistiques mandé 1. pp. 79-107.
sources.quote: [p. 99:] Dans les mots de structures CVCV ou CVNCV : On ne relève que des tendances, les différences, quand il y en a, portant plutôt sur la place de l'accent d'intensité que sur le registre de hauteur tonale. [p. 100:] Dans les mots de structures CVVCV ou CVCCV : Les marques ton/accent sont, à l'inverse, tout à fait nettes et elles restent constantes : a) CVVCV : est toujours accentué sur la 1ère syllabe, registre bas, b) CVCCV : est toujours accentué sur la 1ère syllabe, registre haut [...] il apparaît comme certain que le soninke devait être une langue à tons opposant deux registres [...] ses distinctions tonales se trouvent combinées avec un accent d'intensité.

sources.note: The catalog and Creissels 2015 code Soninke as a tone language with contrastive H vs. L on every syllable (lexical minimal pairs) and mention no stress. Platiel instead holds that the tonal system has lost its distinctive character (only traces survive) and that the language has an intensity accent whose placement is conditioned by syllable structure (heavy CVV or pre-geminate syllable), with lexically variable placement in CVCV words. Both the type (accent vs. contrastive tone) and the existence of word stress differ. Her data come from her own materials and the DNAFLA Soninke-French lexicon…

sources.quote: Kaédi Soninke. sources.citation: Vydrin, Valentin. 2024 [version 2.1, deposited 17 Feb 2025]. Eastern Soninke. sources.quote: Soninke has two level tones: high and low. The only contour tone is HL, it is available on the final syllable of a definite noun before a pause, if the preceding syllable carries a low tone, or in monosyllabic nouns: yàxàrê ‘woman’, sèrê ‘human, person’, sî ‘horse’. ... Two level tonemes can be postulated in Soninke, L and H. ... The HL contour should be interpreted as a combination of two level tonemes, H and L
sources.locator: §3.1 'Character of tonal system', §3.2.1 'Tonemes L and H', §3.2.3 'The non-tonemic status of the HL contour' (docx, no page numbers in the text; c. pp. 4-5)
sources.note: Two level tonemes L and H ('omnitonal', contra Creissels' H = zero); HL fall only derived (floating L of definite article); only L floats; downstep H!H from floating L, downdrift; word patterns H, LH, HL, HLH.. mapped by span rules; no stress. Data: Creissels 2016 (Kingi); 200+ tone-marked forms.

sources.citation: Green, Christopher R. & Maria Konoshenko. 2022. Tonal head marking in Mande compounds: endpoint neutralization and outliers. Mandenkan 67: 3-44. doi:10.4000/mandenkan.2699
sources.quote: Unlike Bozo, a great deal is known about Soninke [iso:snk] and its tonal behavior. Contrary to most other languages discussed so far, in Kingi Soninke, W2 does not neutralize in compounds, as shown in (17). [...] Lack of W2 neutralization in these instances may suggest that Soninke is an outlier with respect to THM. However, THM does occur elsewhere in Soninke, such as in canonical possessive constructions with a referential possessor (18). In possessive constructions, a monosyllabic W2's tone polarizes against W1 as shown in (18a,b), while a non-monosyllabic W2 receives replacive {LH}, cf. (18c,d).
sources.locator: section 4.3 (outliers), paragraphs 66-68 of the OpenEdition HTML (print pp. 3-44), exx. (17)-(18)
sources.note: Full HTML text read: secondhand Kingi Soninke data from Creissels 2016 (46-54, 68-69). Paras 66-68: unlike most Mande languages, Kingi Soninke does not neutralise W2 tone in compounds (ex. 17), but tonal head marking appears in possessive constructions with a referential possessor — a monosyllabic head polarises against the possessor, a longer head takes replacive {LH} (ex. 18); elsewhere the paper notes that a /L/ vs. /Ø/ (marked-L, default-H) analysis has been invoked for Kingi Soninke (Creissels 2016). The word 'numeral' does not occur in the paper.

sources.citation: Creissels, Denis. 2018. Le rôle du ton dans la morphologie flexionnelle du soninké (mandé ouest). In Jean Léo Léonard & Annie Rialland (éds.), Linguistique africaine: perspectives croisées (Journées scientifiques de la Société de Linguistique de Paris, 23 janvier 2016), 163-187. Paris: Éditions de la Société de Linguistique de Paris. ISBN 979-10-699-2586-1.
sources.quote: Comme cela est illustré en (4), le soninké du Kingi a une opposition tonale binaire H vs. B. [...] Ce système présente deux caractéristiques typologiques majeures : (a) En soninké du Kingi, l'unité porteuse de ton est la syllabe, [...] on ne relève aucune différence de comportement entre des syllabes 'légères' et des syllabes 'lourdes'. (b) Le système tonal du soninké du Kingi [...] est un système à ton B marqué, dont on peut simplifier la description en posant que seuls les tons B sont spécifiés en structure sous-jacente, les tons H étant assignés par défaut aux syllabes qui n'ont pas été atteintes par l'expansion d'un domaine de ton bas.
sources.locator: §3.1 'Ton haut et ton bas', pp. 167-168 (the H vs. B sentence and ex. (4) on p. 167; the (a)/(b) typological characteristics on p. 168)
sources.note: Full text (copy consulted) read: binary H vs L opposition with minimal pairs, syllable as TBU regardless of weight, marked-L analysis (only L specified underlyingly, H by default), contour tones and downstep from vowel elision/floating L, lexical tone classes (monosyllabic verbs H vs LH), then a detailed account of substitutive (replacive) morphotonemes — B, H, BH — in verb, noun, adjective, pronoun and numeral inflection.

(b) Le système tonal du soninké du Kingi [...] est un système à ton B marqué, dont on peut simplifier la description en posant que seuls les tons B sont spécifiés en structure sous-jacente, les tons H étant assignés par défaut aux syllabes qui n'ont pas été atteintes par l'expansion d'un domaine de ton bas.

tone.translation: As illustrated in (4), Kingi Soninke has a binary tonal opposition H vs L. [...] This system has two major typological characteristics: (a) in Kingi Soninke the tone-bearing unit is the syllable, [...] there is no difference in behaviour between 'light' and 'heavy' syllables; (b) the Kingi Soninke tone system [...] is a marked-L system, whose description can be simplified by positing that only L tones are specified underlyingly, H tones being assigned by default to syllables not reached by the spreading of a low-tone domain.

sources.citation: Green, Christopher R. 2018. A survey of word-level replacive tonal patterns in Western Mande. Mandenkan 59: 67-108. doi:10.4000/mandenkan.1420
sources.quote: In each instance, unlike what we have come to expect in most Central and Southwestern Mande compounds, in Kingi Soninke, the lexical tonal melody of W2 in a compound is maintained in its entirety, while that of W1 is clearly neutralized. [...] These Kingi Soninke data show, however, that the tonal melody of W1 is always neutralized in favor of its initial tone. For example, in (32a), W1's /LLHL/ melody is neutralized to [LLL], while in (32d), W1's /HLHL/ is neutralized to [HHH]. [...] Thus, in every instance, the neutralized melody of W1 is either all‑H or all‑L, while the melody of W2 is maintained.
sources.locator: section 'Soninke-Bozo', paragraph 128 of the OpenEdition HTML (print pp. 67-108), after ex. (32)
sources.note: Full HTML text read: secondhand (data adapted from Creissels 2016: 46-54). In the 'Soninke-Bozo' section (paras 125-130, ex. 32) Green shows that Kingi Soninke compound tonology differs from Central/Southwestern Mande replacive tone: the first member's lexical melody is neutralised to all-H or all-L (its initial tone spread) while the second member keeps its full lexical melody; he concludes W2 neutralisation is absent in Soninke-Bozo and calls for first-hand tonal description of the branch. No 'partial compacité tonale' examples for Soninke were found in the text.
